title: 22. Interview: Pub/Sub
summary: Interview Q&A for Pub/Sub — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Pub/Sub interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Contrast pub/sub with point-to-point queues. When is each appropriate?
**Answer:** A point-to-point queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer (load-balanced), while pub/sub delivers a copy of each message to every subscriber (fan-out). The two patterns solve different problems. Point-to-point is for parallelizing work: 100 order-processing workers pull from one `orders` queue, each order processed by one worker — total throughput is the sum of worker throughputs. Pub/sub is for event notification: one `order.placed` event is published, and the billing, shipping, notification, and analytics services each receive a copy and react independently. The architect's rule: use a queue when consumers are interchangeable workers on the same task; use pub/sub when consumers are distinct services that each need to react to the same event. The two compose: many systems use a topic for fan-out and a queue per subscriber for load balancing within that subscriber's fleet (the SNS+SQS pattern on AWS, or Kafka topic + Kafka consumer group). Netflix's billing pipeline does exactly this: a Kafka topic fans out to the billing consumer group (10 pods, load-balanced via Kafka partitions) and to the analytics consumer group (50 pods, also load-balanced) — pub/sub across services, point-to-point within each service.
**Visual:**
```
queue (point-to-point):  P -> [Q] -> C1, C2, C3 (one consumer per msg, load-balanced)
pub/sub (fan-out):       P -> [Topic] -> S1 (copy), S2 (copy), S3 (copy)
compose:                 P -> [Topic] -> S1's queue -> S1's workers (load-balanced)
                                     -> S2's queue -> S2's workers
```

### Q2. How does Kafka implement pub/sub when it is fundamentally a partitioned log?
**Answer:** Kafka's pub/sub emerges from the consumer-group abstraction. A topic has N partitions; each partition is an append-only log. Within a single consumer group, partitions are assigned to consumers one-to-one (or one-to-many if there are fewer consumers than partitions), so the group as a whole sees each message exactly once — this is point-to-point / load balancing. Across consumer groups, each group has its own offset cursor on the topic, so each group sees every message — this is pub/sub / fan-out. So Kafka gives you both patterns from the same topic by using different consumer group IDs. To add a new subscriber, you start a new consumer group with a unique ID; it begins consuming from the earliest offset (or latest, configurable) and catches up independently. This is more efficient than separate per-subscriber queues because the topic's data is stored once on disk, and each consumer group reads its own copy from the OS page cache (zero-copy sendfile), so fan-out does not multiply disk I/O. The trade-off is that partition count limits parallelism per consumer group (a group with more consumers than partitions has idle consumers), so the topic must be partitioned for the largest consumer group's parallelism needs.
**Visual:**
```
topic T with 4 partitions P0..P3:
  group "recs":   C1 <- P0,P1   C2 <- P2,P3   (load-balanced within group)
  group "anal":   C3 <- P0,P1   C4 <- P2,P3   (sees same msgs as "recs")
  group "bill":   C5 <- P0..P3  (single consumer, sees all msgs)
each group has independent offset cursor -> pub/sub across groups
topic stored once on disk; groups read from page cache (zero-copy)
```

### Q3. What is the difference between durable and ephemeral pub/sub? Give an example of each.
**Answer:** Durable pub/sub persists messages until every subscriber has acked (or until retention expires), so a subscriber that is offline when a message is published receives it on reconnect. Ephemeral pub/sub delivers messages only to subscribers that are currently connected; an offline subscriber misses the message permanently. Durable examples: Google Pub/Sub (messages retained 7 days by default, ack-based), AWS SNS+SQS (SNS fans out to SQS queues that persist until consumed), Kafka (log retention, days to weeks). These are used for any subscriber whose missing a message has consequences — billing, analytics, audit. Ephemeral examples: Redis Pub/Sub (pushes to currently-connected subscribers, no persistence), MQTT (used in IoT, where stale sensor readings are noise), WebSocket-based live updates (a sports score feed where the latest value is all that matters). The trade-off is latency vs durability: ephemeral systems deliver in <1ms because there is no disk write; durable systems deliver in 5–50ms because of the persistence round-trip. The architect's rule: default to durable for anything that affects business state; use ephemeral only for transient push where the consumer can tolerate (or prefers) missing messages while offline. Mixing the two — durable for the audit trail, ephemeral for the live UI — is common.
**Visual:**
```
durable:    publish -> [broker persists] -> sub1 acks, sub2 offline
            sub2 reconnects -> receives missed msgs (within retention)
            Google Pub/Sub, SNS+SQS, Kafka (5-50ms latency)
ephemeral:  publish -> broker pushes to currently-connected subs only
            sub2 offline -> MISSES msg forever
            Redis Pub/Sub, MQTT (<1ms latency)
use durable: billing, analytics, audit, state changes
use ephemeral: live presence, sports scores, chat typing indicators
```

### Q4. How do you ensure per-key ordering in pub/sub with multiple subscribers?
**Answer:** Per-key ordering requires that all messages with the same key are delivered to the same consumer in the same order they were produced. In Kafka, this is automatic: the producer sets a partition key (e.g., `user_id`), the broker hashes the key to a partition, and within a partition messages are in append order. Each consumer group has one consumer per partition, so that consumer sees the user's events in order. Across subscribers (different consumer groups), each group independently reads the same partition in order, so per-key ordering is preserved for every subscriber. In Google Pub/Sub, you set an `orderingKey` on publish, and the broker guarantees that messages with the same key are delivered to the same subscriber in order — but at the cost of reduced throughput (the key's messages serialize). In SNS FIFO, you set a `MessageGroupId`, and within a group messages are ordered. The trade-off is that ordering costs parallelism: a single hot key serializes through one partition/subscriber, capping that key's throughput. The architect's rule: choose a partition key that is fine-grained enough to spread load but coarse enough to preserve the ordering you need — `user_id` for per-user ordering, `order_id` for per-order ordering, never `null` (which randomizes and loses all ordering). For total ordering across all keys, you must use a single partition, which caps throughput at one consumer's rate.
**Visual:**
```
Kafka: key=user_id -> hash -> partition P0
  all user_id=alice msgs -> P0 -> one consumer in group -> ordered
  group "recs" sees P0 in order; group "bill" sees P0 in order (independent)
Google Pub/Sub: orderingKey=user_id -> serialized for that key
SNS FIFO: MessageGroupId=order_id -> ordered within group
hot key (e.g., celebrity user_id) serializes -> throughput cap for that key
```

### Q5. What is the cost of fan-out, and how do you scale pub/sub for many subscribers?
**Answer:** Fan-out multiplies outbound bandwidth by the subscriber count: one published message becomes N copies. For a topic with 1MB/sec ingress and 100 subscribers, the broker pushes 100MB/sec outbound, which saturates network links and broker CPU. Three scaling strategies. First, **shared transport**: Kafka stores the topic once on disk and each consumer group reads from the OS page cache via zero-copy `sendfile`, so fan-out does not multiply disk I/O — outbound network is still 100MB/sec but disk and CPU are bounded. This is why Kafka scales to thousands of consumer groups per topic. Second, **selective subscription**: instead of N subscribers each filtering the topic, use topic partitioning or header-based filtering so subscribers only receive messages they care about. AWS EventBridge and Kafka's `KTable` filtering let subscribers express interest in `event_type=order.placed AND region=us-east-1`, reducing per-subscriber bandwidth. Third, **hierarchical fan-out**: a "spoke" subscriber receives the topic and republishes to a regional broker, so cross-region bandwidth is 1× not N×. Netflix does this: a global Kafka topic fans out to a per-region Kafka topic, and regional subscribers consume locally. The architect's rule: monitor outbound bandwidth per subscriber and per topic; if outbound exceeds the broker's network capacity, shard the topic or move to hierarchical fan-out. The mistake is to assume fan-out is free — at 100+ subscribers it dominates the broker's resource budget.
**Visual:**
```
1 MB/s ingress, 100 subs -> 100 MB/s outbound (broker bottleneck)
fix 1: Kafka zero-copy (page cache -> network, no per-sub disk read)
fix 2: selective subscription (EventBridge filters: only order.placed in us-east)
fix 3: hierarchical: global topic -> regional topic -> local subs (1x cross-region)
monitor: outbound MB/s per subscriber, alert at 70% of broker NIC capacity
```

### Q6. How do subscribers handle back-pressure independently in pub/sub?
**Answer:** Each subscriber has its own queue (or offset cursor) and applies its own back-pressure without affecting other subscribers or the producer. In Kafka, a slow consumer simply stops advancing its offset; the broker does not push, so there is no back-pressure on the broker or producer — the consumer's lag grows but the broker is fine. In Google Pub/Sub and SNS+SQS, the subscriber's subscription queue grows; if it exceeds the retention window (7 days for Pub/Sub, 4 days for SQS), messages are dropped, so the subscriber must keep up or accept data loss. The producer is unaffected because the broker acks the publish independently of subscriber progress. The architect's monitoring focus is per-subscriber lag: a subscriber whose lag grows linearly indicates a throughput problem (scale the subscriber fleet); a subscriber whose lag spikes and recovers indicates a transient burst (acceptable); a subscriber whose lag grows unboundedly indicates a bug or undersized fleet (page). Netflix's dashboards show per-subscriber lag for every consumer group, with SLOs like "billing lag < 30 seconds, analytics lag < 5 minutes." The rule: per-subscriber SLOs, per-subscriber alerts, per-subscriber autoscaling — never average lag across subscribers, because an averaged metric hides a starving subscriber.
**Visual:**
```
producer -> [topic] -> sub1 queue (lag: 0s, healthy)
                    -> sub2 queue (lag: 5 min, slow but OK)
                    -> sub3 queue (lag: growing linearly -> page)
back-pressure is per-subscriber; producer never slows
monitor: per-subscriber lag, not average; SLO: billing<30s, analytics<5min
autoscale: lag > threshold -> add pods to that subscriber's fleet only
```

### Q7. What is the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once delivery in pub/sub, and how is exactly-once achieved?
**Answer:** At-least-once delivery means each subscriber receives every message at least once, but may receive duplicates (typically due to redelivery after a crash or a network retry). Exactly-once delivery means each subscriber receives every message exactly once, with no duplicates and no losses. At-least-once is the default for Kafka, Google Pub/Sub, and SNS+SQS; it requires subscribers to be idempotent (dedup on `event_id`). Exactly-once is harder: it requires transactional semantics across the broker and the subscriber's side-effect store. Kafka achieves it via the transactional producer/consumer API (KIP-98): the producer wraps a set of publishes and consumer-offset commits in a transaction, and the consumer is configured with `isolation.level=read_committed` so it sees only committed transactions. This gives exactly-once stream processing (Kafka Streams uses it natively), but at the cost of 2x–3x latency and significant operational complexity. Google Pub/Sub offers exactly-once via a deduplication window on the subscriber side, but it is not a true transactional guarantee. The architect's rule: default to at-least-once with idempotent subscribers (use a unique `event_id` and a dedup table), because it is simple, fast, and correct in practice. Reserve exactly-once for the rare case where dedup is impossible (e.g., an external side effect like sending an SMS) and the cost of duplicates is unacceptable.
**Visual:**
```
at-least-once (default): sub may receive dup -> must dedup on event_id
  Kafka, Google Pub/Sub, SNS+SQS: simple, fast, idempotency required
exactly-once (rare): txn(publish + offset_commit) + read_committed
  Kafka 0.11+ (KIP-98): 2-3x latency, complex, used for stream processing
rule: default at-least-once + idempotent sub; exactly-once only when dedup impossible
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix's "video viewed" event is published to a Kafka topic and consumed by 5 consumer groups: recommendations, analytics, billing, fraud, and notifications. The fraud consumer falls behind by 2 hours. What is the impact and how do you respond?
**Answer:** The fraud consumer's lag has no impact on the other 4 consumer groups (Kafka isolates groups via independent offsets) or on the producer (the broker acks publishes independently of consumer progress). The fraud consumer's lag means fraud detection is delayed by 2 hours, which may be acceptable (fraud is often detected post-event) or unacceptable (real-time chargeback prevention). The response has three steps. First, diagnose: is the lag growing linearly (throughput problem, fleet undersized) or spiking (transient burst, possibly a downstream dependency slowness)? Linear growth means scale the fleet; spiking means investigate the dependency. Second, scale: add pods to the fraud consumer group (HPA on `kafka_consumergroup_lag`). Kafka will rebalance partitions to the new pods, briefly pausing consumption during the rebalance (a few seconds). Third, prevent recurrence: set per-subscriber SLOs (fraud lag < 5 minutes) and alerts; if the fraud workload is bursty, size the fleet for peak rate × 1.5. If the fraud consumer genuinely cannot keep up at peak, consider a separate fraud-specific topic with fewer partitions (lower per-pod overhead) or a sampling strategy (process only high-risk events in real time, batch-process the rest). The architect's rule: per-subscriber SLOs and autoscaling are the operational contract of pub/sub — without them, one slow subscriber silently degrades the business.
**Visual:**
```
5 consumer groups, fraud lags 2h:
  impact: ONLY fraud detection delayed; other 4 groups + producer unaffected
respond:
  1. diagnose: linear growth -> scale; spike -> check downstream dep
  2. HPA on lag -> add fraud pods -> rebalance (brief pause) -> catch up
  3. prevent: SLO fraud lag < 5min; alert at 1min; size for peak*1.5
  4. if can't keep up: separate fraud topic, sampling, or batch fallback
```

### Q2. You use SNS+SQS for fan-out: SNS topic fans out to 3 SQS queues (billing, shipping, notifications). The shipping queue's messages are stuck because the shipping consumer is down. The other 2 queues are draining fine. How do you handle this without losing messages?
**Answer:** SNS fans out by writing a copy of each message to each SQS queue, and each queue is independent — so the billing and notification queues drain normally while the shipping queue accumulates. The shipping queue's messages are not lost (SQS retains messages for 4 days by default, up to 14 days maximum), so the immediate priority is to restore the shipping consumer before retention expires. Three responses. First, fix the consumer: if it is a crashed pod, Kubernetes will restart it; if it is a code bug, deploy a fix. The queue continues to accumulate during the fix, which is fine as long as retention is not exceeded. Second, scale up once the consumer is healthy: the queue may have 100k+ messages, and the consumer's normal fleet may take hours to drain — add pods (or increase concurrency) to drain faster. Third, monitor retention: if the queue depth × processing time exceeds 4 days, raise the retention to 14 days via `SetQueueAttributes` to buy time. Long-term, set per-queue alerts: queue depth > 10k (warning), > 100k (page), and approximate age of oldest message > 1 day (page). The architect's rule: SNS+SQS isolates subscribers by design — a down subscriber does not affect others — but each subscription must be monitored independently, because no one else will notice the silent accumulation.
**Visual:**
```
SNS topic -> [billing Q] -> billing consumer (healthy, draining)
          -> [shipping Q] -> shipping consumer DOWN (Q grows, 4d retention)
          -> [notif Q] -> notif consumer (healthy, draining)
respond:
  1. fix shipping consumer (k8s restart or deploy fix)
  2. scale up to drain backlog (100k msgs, add pods)
  3. raise retention to 14d if needed (buy time)
alerts: depth>10k warn, >100k page, oldest_age>1d page
```

### Q3. Spotify publishes "track played" events to Google Pub/Sub for fan-out to royalty accounting, recommendation training, and the real-time dashboard. The dashboard subscriber is in a different region with high latency. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** Cross-region pub/sub has two costs: the publish round-trip (producer to broker) and the pull round-trip (subscriber to broker). If the dashboard subscriber is in a different region from the topic, every pull incurs the cross-region round-trip latency (50–200ms), and high-frequency pulls (every 100ms for real-time) saturate the cross-region link. Three optimizations. First, **regional topic replication**: replicate the topic to the dashboard's region (Google Pub/Sub's `Topic` with multi-region, or Kafka MirrorMaker/Cluster Linking), so the dashboard pulls from a local topic with <5ms latency. The cross-region bandwidth is 1× (one replication stream) instead of N× (N pulls per second from the remote region). Second, **batched pulls**: the dashboard pulls 1000 messages per request with `maxMessages` and `returnImmediately=false`, so the round-trip cost is amortized over 1000 messages — the per-message latency drops from 100ms to 0.1ms. Third, **push delivery**: switch the dashboard subscription from pull to push (Google Pub/Sub delivers via HTTP POST to a regional endpoint), so the broker initiates delivery and the subscriber's regional endpoint responds locally. The trade-off: push requires the subscriber to be a public HTTP endpoint (security review), while pull keeps the subscriber behind a VPC. The architect's rule: for cross-region subscribers, replicate the topic locally and use push or batched pull — never high-frequency single-message pulls across regions.
**Visual:**
```
producer (region A) -> topic (region A)
  dashboard sub (region B) pulls every 100ms -> 100ms latency, N× bandwidth
optimize:
  1. replicate topic to region B (1x bandwidth, local pulls)
  2. batched pulls (maxMessages=1000, returnImmediately=false) -> 0.1ms/msg
  3. push delivery to regional HTTP endpoint (broker initiates, local response)
trade-off: push needs public endpoint; pull keeps sub in VPC
```

### Q4. Uber's "trip completed" event fans out to 8 consumer groups. The billing consumer must not lose any messages, but the analytics consumer can tolerate 0.1% loss. How do you configure retention and ack differently?
**Answer:** Different subscribers have different durability requirements, and Kafka's per-consumer-group offset model accommodates this naturally. For the billing consumer: configure a long topic retention (7 days minimum, 30 days preferred) so that even if the billing consumer is down for a day, it can catch up on reconnect; set the consumer's `auto.offset.reset=earliest` so a new consumer group starts from the beginning (no skips); commit offsets only after the billing write is durably committed (ack after DB commit, not before); and alert on billing lag > 30 seconds. For the analytics consumer: configure shorter retention (24 hours) to save broker storage; set `auto.offset.reset=latest` so a new consumer group starts from "now" (skips historical); commit offsets periodically (every 5 seconds) without waiting for processing, accepting that a crash loses the in-flight batch (0.1% loss is acceptable); and alert on analytics lag > 5 minutes. The broker's retention is the maximum of all subscribers' needs (7 days, because billing needs it), so the analytics consumer does not save storage at the broker — but its own consumer behavior (skip-on-restart, periodic commit) is what enables the lossy semantic. The architect's rule: durability is per-subscriber via offset management, not per-topic; the topic's retention must satisfy the most durability-sensitive subscriber.
**Visual:**
```
topic retention: 7 days (max of all subs' needs)
billing sub:
  auto.offset.reset=earliest (no skips)
  commit offset AFTER DB commit (no loss on crash)
  alert: lag > 30s
analytics sub:
  auto.offset.reset=latest (skip historical on restart, ~0.1% loss OK)
  commit every 5s (crash loses in-flight batch, acceptable)
  alert: lag > 5min
durability is per-subscriber via offset behavior, not per-topic
```

### Q5. You use Redis Pub/Sub for a chat presence system (who is online). A subscriber reconnects after a 30-second network blip and has missed presence updates. Is this acceptable, and what would change if you used Redis Streams instead?
**Answer:** For a chat presence system, missing 30 seconds of updates is usually acceptable: presence is a "current state" signal, and the subscriber can re-fetch the current presence list on reconnect (a separate `GET presence:*` call), so the missed intermediate updates are irrelevant — what matters is the current state, not the transitions. This is the canonical use case for ephemeral pub/sub: low latency (<1ms), no persistence, and the consumer recomputes state on reconnect. Redis Pub/Sub is correct here. If you switched to Redis Streams (a durable, Kafka-like log with consumer groups), you would gain durability (the reconnecting subscriber receives the 30 seconds of missed updates) but at the cost of higher latency (each publish writes to disk) and higher storage (presence history accumulates, requiring periodic trimming). For presence, this is wasted work — the subscriber does not need the history. The architect's rule: classify the workload. "Current state" workloads (presence, live scores, stock tickers) suit ephemeral pub/sub; "event log" workloads (chat messages, audit trails, state transitions) suit durable pub/sub. Using durable for current-state is over-engineering; using ephemeral for event-log is data loss. Many chat systems use both: ephemeral for presence, durable (Kafka or Redis Streams) for the actual messages.
**Visual:**
```
presence (current state):  ephemeral Redis Pub/Sub -> 30s blip OK, re-fetch on reconnect
  subscriber: GET presence:* on reconnect -> current state, history irrelevant
chat messages (event log): durable Kafka / Redis Streams -> 30s blip -> receive missed msgs
  subscriber: resume from last committed offset, no loss
rule: current-state -> ephemeral; event-log -> durable; many systems use both
```

### Q6. WhatsApp delivers messages to recipients who may be offline. They use a durable pub/sub per recipient. How do they handle a recipient whose phone is offline for 30 days?
**Answer:** A recipient offline for 30 days presents two problems: storage cost (their pending messages accumulate in the broker) and delivery on reconnect (the broker must replay 30 days of messages without overwhelming the phone or the network). The pattern WhatsApp uses has three layers. First, **per-recipient queue with bounded retention**: each recipient has a queue (or a partition keyed by `recipient_id`) with a retention that matches the business SLA — typically 30 days for personal messages, longer for verified accounts. Messages older than retention are expired (or archived to cold storage). Second, **batched delivery on reconnect**: when the recipient's phone reconnects, the broker delivers pending messages in batches (10–100 per round trip) with exponential backoff if the phone is slow to ack, avoiding a thundering-herd that overwhelms the phone's CPU or battery. Third, **priority for recent messages**: the broker delivers the most recent N messages first (so the user sees their latest conversations immediately), then backfills older messages in the background. The architect's rule: long-offline recipients are a storage and delivery problem, not just a delivery problem; design for bounded retention, batched catch-up, and priority for recent state. WhatsApp's blog confirms this: their per-user storage is capped, expired messages are archived, and reconnection uses a "fetch recent first, backfill older" protocol that delivers a usable UI within seconds of reconnect.
**Visual:**
```
recipient offline 30 days -> queue accumulates (bounded retention 30d)
on reconnect:
  1. deliver most recent N=50 msgs first (user sees latest immediately)
  2. backfill older msgs in batches of 10-100, exp backoff if slow ack
  3. expire msgs older than 30d (or archive to cold storage)
storage: per-recipient queue, capped; long-offline users cost disk
UI: usable within seconds (recent first), full history in background
```

### Q7. Amazon's product-page service subscribes to "price changed" events to update its in-memory cache. The subscriber is a fleet of 1000 cache pods. How do you avoid sending every price change to all 1000 pods?
**Answer:** Sending every price change to all 1000 cache pods is wasteful: most pods do not have the affected product in their cache, so the message is a no-op. Three patterns to avoid the waste. First, **selective subscription**: instead of one "price changed" topic that all pods subscribe to, partition the topic by `product_id` and have each pod subscribe only to partitions corresponding to products it caches. This requires the pod to know which products it caches (a consistent-hash mapping from `product_id` to pod, so each product is owned by one pod), and the broker routes only relevant messages. Second, **filter at the broker**: AWS EventBridge and Kafka 2.8+ support header-based filtering, where the subscriber expresses interest in `product_id IN (cached_set)` and the broker delivers only matching messages. Third, **filter at the subscriber with coalescing**: all 1000 pods subscribe, but each pod's consumer checks "is this product in my cache?" and discards if not; additionally, coalesce rapid updates (only the latest price for a product matters, so a pod that receives 10 price changes for the same product in 100ms processes only the last). The architect's rule: for fan-out to large fleets with selective interest, partition by ownership (cheapest) or filter at the broker (most flexible); subscriber-side filtering is a fallback when the broker cannot filter. Amazon's actual pattern uses consistent-hash partitioning: each product is owned by 3 pods (for redundancy), and price changes route to those 3 pods only.
**Visual:**
```
naive: 1 topic -> 1000 pods subscribe -> each pod gets every price change (wasteful)
fix 1: partition by product_id, pod subscribes only to its partitions
        (consistent hash: product -> 3 pods -> only they receive)
fix 2: broker-side filter (EventBridge: product_id IN cached_set)
fix 3: subscriber-side filter + coalesce (only latest price per product matters)
Amazon: consistent-hash, 3 pods per product, route to only those 3
```
